title: Appraising Evidence for Hippocampal Synaptic Restoration by Traditional Chinese Medicine-Derived Antidepressant Interventions: Causality, Exposure, and Translation.
abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-derived interventions have been associated with antidepressant-like behavioral effects and changes in markers of hippocampal plasticity, but evidence of functional synaptic recovery remains limited. This critical narrative review evaluates 29 purposively selected preclinical reports using six qualitative appraisal domains: mechanistic causality, independent replication, anatomical resolution, methodological reporting, central target exposure, and clinical translation. The selected reports examined interventions including Yueju, Xiaoyaosan, ginsenoside Rb1, baicalin, and danshensu in stress-based models and behavioral screening paradigms. Behavioral effects and changes in AMPA receptor-associated signaling, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its receptor tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), and synaptic proteins were frequently reported; however, these findings cannot substitute for direct measurements of synaptic physiology. Studies of repeated-dose Rb1 and baicalin reported hippocampal cornu ammonis area 1 (CA1) long-term potentiation (LTP). In the Rb1 study, miR-134 perturbation was tested against the LTP endpoint, whereas TrkB inhibition in the baicalin study was evaluated against behavioral outcomes in separate experiments. Zhi-Zi-Chi-Tang (ZZCT) was also associated with improved CA1 LTP, but 14-3-3ζ knockdown was not tested against that functional endpoint. Unclear animal-versus-slice denominators, limited data on unbound hippocampal exposure, and insufficient independent replication constrain causal inference. Overall, the selected evidence supports specific functional findings and mechanistic associations but does not establish a shared, causally validated pathway for hippocampal synaptic restoration.

title: Tirzepatide Attenuates Cortical Inflammatory and Neuronal Alterations in Diabetic Rats: Associations with PI3K/AKT Phosphorylation and Conditioned Fear Responses.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Tirzepatide lowers blood glucose, but its effects on diabetes-associated neurological dysfunction remain incompletely characterized. We examined conditioned fear responses and accompanying prefrontal cortical alterations in diabetic rats. Methods: Male Sprague Dawley rats with diabetes induced by a high-fat diet and streptozotocin received tirzepatide (1.35 mg/kg intraperitoneally, twice weekly) for 10 weeks. Metabolic and behavioral assessments included eight rats per group. Neuronal morphology, synapse-associated proteins, tau phosphorylation, inflammatory cytokines, PI3K/AKT phosphorylation, and autophagy-related proteins were examined in prefrontal cortical tissue. Results: Tirzepatide treatment was associated with improved glycemic control and oral glucose tolerance. The insulin-tolerance-test area under the curve did not differ significantly between treated and untreated diabetic rats (adjusted p = 0.0993). Treated diabetic rats showed higher freezing at 96 h (adjusted p = 0.0017), although the group-by-time interaction was not significant (p = 0.1308). Treatment was associated with fewer neurons showing degeneration-like morphology, higher PSD95 and SYT1 abundance, and lower tau phosphorylation at Thr205 and Ser404. Prefrontal cortical TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β expression decreased. Prefrontal cortical TNF-α and IL-1β mRNA levels and protein concentrations of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β were lower following tirzepatide treatment, whereas the reduction in IL-6 mRNA was not statistically significant. PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and the abundance of autophagy-related proteins were also altered. Conclusions: The findings link tirzepatide treatment to metabolic, behavioral, inflammatory, and neuronal changes in diabetic rats. They do not establish PI3K/AKT causality, restored autophagic flux, or restored long-term memory. Direct central effects cannot be separated from the consequences of improved systemic metabolism. Initial conditioning differences and the absence of independent locomotor and shock-sensitivity assessments limit the behavioral interpretation. Nissl morphology and synaptic protein abundance do not independently establish neuronal viability or improved synaptic function.

title: The Role of Psychostimulants in the Management of Refractory Catatonia: A Comprehensive Review of Case Reports.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterised by motor, behavioural, and affective abnormalities and is frequently associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive and bipolar disorders. Although benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy are considered first-line treatments, a substantial proportion of patients show partial or no response, especially in chronic, affective, or medically complex presentations. Contemporary neurobiological models implicate dysfunction across multiple neurotransmitter systems, including GABAergic, glutamatergic, and dopaminergic pathways, as well as disturbances in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits involved in psychomotor control and arousal regulation. Within this framework, psychostimulants may exert therapeutic effects by enhancing dopaminergic and noradrenergic transmission, thereby modulating frontal-striatal networks and facilitating behavioural activation and motor initiation. Evidence from conditions characterised by psychomotor slowing, apathy, and impaired behavioural initiation provides a neurophysiological rationale for their adjunctive use in selected cases of catatonia, particularly when associated with mood disorders. However, there is a dearth of empirical data, with the evidence largely confined to case reports, hence the need for comprehensive reviews of cases and controlled studies to clarify the role of psychostimulants and to explore drug combinations in the treatment of catatonia. Methods: We conducted a comprehensive review of case reports on 22 October 2026 on PubMed, Scopus, PsycInfo/PsycArticles, and Web of Science. Results: We included 9 studies. Psychostimulants were usually helpful in inducing rapid symptoms resolution of catatonia. Conclusions: Psychostimulants may be used in cases of catatonia and provide rapid improvement. Future longitudinal, double-blind designs are likely to allow reliably assessing the value of psychostimulants in catatonia.

title: Integrated Experimental and Computational Discovery of the Oxazole-Thiadiazole-Sulfonamide Hybrids as Dual α-Amylase and α-Glucosidase Inhibitors.
abstract: Background: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a major global health concern. Inhibition of α-amylase and α-glucosidase is an established approach to controlling postprandial glucose levels. In this study, we aimed to synthesize oxazole-thiadiazole-sulphonamide derivatives (1-14) and evaluate their inhibitory activity against both enzymes. Methods: Fourteen derivatives were synthesized and characterized using 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and high-resolution electron ionization mass spectrometry (HR-EI-MS). Their inhibitory activities were evaluated using acarbose as the reference inhibitor. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis and molecular docking studies were performed to investigate the influence of aromatic substitution and explore potential enzyme-ligand interactions. Results: Compound 5 had the strongest inhibitory activity, displaying values of IC50 6.20 ± 0.30 µM for α-amylase and 6.70 ± 0.20 µM for α-glucosidase, in comparison with 10.50 ± 0.20 µM and 11.10 ± 0.30 µM, respectively, for acarbose. The other derivatives showed varying inhibitory activities. Docking analysis provided computational insights into possible interactions within the enzyme binding sites. Conclusions: Compound 5 was the most potent derivative in the series against both enzymes and represents a promising in vitro candidate for further biochemical, mechanistic, and safety evaluation.

title: MicroRNAs in Alzheimer's Disease: From Molecular Pathogenesis to Biomarkers and Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline due to accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques outside neurons and neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons. The polygenic, multifactorial nature of the disease has limited the efficacy of single-target therapeutics and has shifted interest towards agents that act on several pathological pathways. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are well suited to this purpose: they are small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally, and a single miRNA can regulate many transcripts within a common pathway. Since their first identification, appreciation of their regulatory capacity in the healthy and diseased brain has grown substantially and altered miRNA expression is now linked to a range of neurodegenerative diseases. In AD, selected miRNAs have been associated with amyloidogenic APP processing, BACE1 expression, tau phosphorylation, apolipoprotein E lipidation and neuroinflammation. Circulating miRNA signatures in blood and cerebrospinal fluid are being explored as minimally invasive diagnostic biomarkers alongside established plasma phosphorylated tau and Aβ42/40 measures. More recently, attention has turned to the therapeutic potential of these molecules, with crossing the blood-brain barrier remaining the major hurdle. This review summarizes the biogenesis and mechanism of action of miRNAs and critically assesses their emerging value as biomarkers and therapeutic candidates.

title: Pharmacokinetics and Effect of Novel Sydnonimine on NO and cGMP Accumulation In Vivo.
abstract: Background: Sydnonimines are mesoionic heterocyclic NO donors with vasodilatory activity. Molsidomine, a clinically approved sydnonimine, has limited blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, restricting its use for cerebrovascular disorders. This study characterizes the lead compound BBP2023 as a potential NO donor with putative cerebral action. Methods: In silico ADME profiling (RDKit) of 14 sydnonimines, rat pharmacokinetics of oral BBP2023 (11 mg/kg) vs. molsidomine (10.4 mg/kg), HPLC-MS/MS of NO/cGMP, and docking against four human sGC PDB entries were performed. Results: BBP2023 showed high lipophilicity (logP 1.58), low TPSA (69.78 Å2) and predicted high BBB permeability. After oral dosing, BBP2023 was rapidly absorbed (plasma Tmax 0.17 h, Cmax 389 ng/mL, AUC_last 235 h·ng/mL) and extensively distributed, with highest exposure in liver (AUC_last 1457 h·ng/mL, ~6-fold plasma), indicating primary hepatic metabolism. Brain penetration was confirmed (fr = 1.39, MRT 3.01 h). The active metabolite BBP2023 A appeared later (plasma Tmax 1.00 h, Cmax 22 ng/mL) and accumulated in the lungs (fr = 25.31, AUC_last 1569 h·ng/mL) and brain (fr = 3.65, MRT 4.16 h). Compared with molsidomine, BBP2023 achieved higher brain exposure (availability 1.4 vs. 0.2, Cmax 852.5 vs. 142.3 pmol/mL) and faster brain Tmax (≤0.25 h vs. 1 h). BBP2023 significantly increased NO and cGMP in the brain (131.00 ± 26.39 nM/g and 1070.83 ± 92.04 pM/g, respectively), whereas molsidomine predominantly elevated heart NO. Docking and MM-GBSA calculations suggested possible interactions of BBP2023 and its metabolites with the sGC stimulator site and associated the intact sydnonimine ring with more favorable calculated scores. Conclusions: BBP2023 acts as a NO donor with favorable pharmacokinetics, effective BBB penetration, and brain NO/cGMP accumulation, supporting its further development for cerebrovascular disorders.

title: Targeting Autophagy with Puerarin: From a Natural Isoflavone to Therapeutic Applications.
abstract: Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved lysosomal degradation process that eliminates damaged organelles and misfolded proteins to maintain cellular homeostasis. Its dysfunction drives cancer, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular, hepatic, renal and skeletal muscle disorders, making autophagy a promising therapeutic target. Puerarin, a characteristic isoflavone from the leguminous medicinal plant Pueraria lobata, exerts broad pharmacological functions via autophagy modulation, yet no systematic review summarizes its tissue-specific regulatory patterns. This narrative review collects and categorizes recent cellular and animal studies on puerarin-autophagy crosstalk from mainstream databases. It organizes puerarin's bidirectional autophagy effects across multiple organs and summarizes core signaling pathways, including AMPK/mTOR and PI3K/Akt/mTOR. Puerarin exhibits context-dependent dual regulation of autophagy: it induces protective autophagy to relieve metabolic and degenerative organ injuries, while inhibiting excessive autophagy to alleviate fibrosis and tumor progression. Its regulatory roles depend on Nrf2, JNK/Beclin1 and mitophagy-related axes in cardiac, hepatic, pulmonary, renal, bone, muscle and nervous tissues, as well as various tumor models. These mechanistic insights may support the development of natural isoflavone-based therapeutic strategies targeting autophagy and broaden the value-added utilization of Pueraria lobata as a medicinal and agricultural resource.

title: Mitochondria-Related Protein Abundance Changes Following Tianeptine Treatment in Rats Exposed to Chronic Social Isolation: A Focused Narrative Review.
abstract: Chronic psychosocial stress contributes to depression and has been associated with changes in mitochondrial function and cellular energy metabolism. Tianeptine (Tian), an atypical antidepressant, has been shown to modulate stress-related behavioral and molecular adaptations, but its effects on hippocampal mitochondrial proteins remain insufficiently characterized. This focused narrative review summarizes findings from two previously published proteomic datasets obtained using the same rat model of chronic social isolation (CSIS) stress, an animal model of depression. The datasets examined Tian-associated changes in hippocampal protein abundance in nonsynaptic mitochondria (NSM) and mitochondria-related proteins detected in the synaptosome-enriched fraction. Increased abundance was reported for proteins associated with oxidative phosphorylation, ATP synthesis, and mitochondrial transport across the two fractions, although voltage-dependent anion channel 1 was the only protein showing increased abundance in both. Changes in the abundance of proteins associated with pyruvate oxidation differed between the fractions, with decreases reported in NSM and increases among the mitochondria-related proteins detected in the synaptosome-enriched fraction. Glutamate dehydrogenase abundance decreased in NSM but increased in the synaptosome-enriched fraction. Other changes in NSM involved proteins associated with amino acid transport, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, redox homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and mitochondrial gene expression. In the synaptosome-enriched fraction, additional changes involved mitochondria-related proteins associated with protein quality control/proteostasis and antioxidant defense, as well as proteins involved in synaptic membrane trafficking. Overall, comparison of the two datasets revealed overlapping and divergent patterns of protein-abundance changes, suggesting that the proteomic alterations associated with chronic Tian treatment in CSIS rats vary across hippocampal subcellular fractions.

title: RepurposeAD: Knowledge Graph-Guided LLM Reasoning for Alzheimer's Drug Repurposing.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer's disease (AD) drug development continues to suffer from high late-stage attrition and narrow mechanistic diversity, which makes the systematic repurposing of approved compounds an urgent priority. Existing computational repurposing methods operate on fragmented biomedical knowledge, rarely integrate transcriptomic and pharmacological evidence within a single reasoning process, and provide little of the mechanistic transparency required for clinical translation. This paper presents RepurposeAD, a knowledge graph-guided large language model (LLM) reasoning framework that identifies and ranks repurposed candidates for AD. Methods: RepurposeAD constructs a unified AD-centric knowledge graph from protein interaction networks, drug-target databases, clinical trial registries, and transcriptomic signatures, linking genetic risk loci, amyloid and tau pathway nodes, neuroinflammatory mediators, and established therapeutic mechanisms. A constrained multi-hop path reasoning module scores drug-to-disease routes and attributes each route to one of five pathological axes, after which an LLM-based evidence synthesis module reads the retrieved paths, trial records, and literature to produce calibrated mechanistic justifications and a final iterative re-ranking. Results: On a curated benchmark of 1847 drug-disease associations spanning amyloid, tau, neuroinflammatory, synaptic, and metabolic targets, RepurposeAD attains a top-10 hit rate of 0.83, an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.79, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.93, and a mean reciprocal rank of 0.65, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 0.07 in hit rate and 0.08 in precision-recall area. Three of the ten highest ranked candidates have active or completed trials in AD-adjacent indications. Conclusions: RepurposeAD provides a transparent, scalable, and mechanistically grounded pipeline for accelerating repurposing in AD and related dementias.

title: Brivaracetam in Off-Label Use and Special Populations: A Narrative Review of Current Evidence.
abstract: Background: Brivaracetam (BRV) is a synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A) ligand approved for the treatment of focal-onset seizures. Its clinical use has increasingly expanded beyond approved indications and into understudied populations. Objective: We aim to review BRV use beyond approved indications and in special populations. Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to 30 April 2026. Eligible clinical studies were selected using prespecified criteria and synthesized narratively. Off-label status was determined separately under FDA and EMA labelling. Results: The evidence consisted predominantly of observational studies, real-world cohorts, case series, and subgroup analyses of randomised trials. In genetic generalized epilepsies (GGE), BRV was associated with seizure reduction in several cohorts, whereas findings in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) were more heterogeneous. Real-world studies demonstrated the feasibility of BRV monotherapy, particularly following transition from levetiracetam. In status epilepticus (SE), intravenous BRV has been associated with SE cessation, although its independent contribution, optimal dose and timing, and role in treatment algorithms remain uncertain. Pregnancy and breastfeeding reports identified no clear safety signal, although exposure and long-term outcome data were scarce. Neonatal evidence was restricted largely to pharmacokinetic and short-term tolerability findings. Observational data indicated that psychiatric or behavioural adverse effects did not recur in some patients switched from levetiracetam; evidence in psychotic disorders remained particularly limited. Conclusions: BRV may be useful in selected off-label settings and special populations. However, evidence remains limited and largely observational, so treatment decisions should be individualized. Prospective controlled studies and dedicated registries are needed.

title: Deferasirox, an Oral Iron Chelator, Confers Antidepressant and Procognitive Effects in a Rat Model of Depression: Hippocampal Ferroptosis, Synaptopathy, and Neurodegeneration.
abstract: Background: Disrupted iron homeostasis is increasingly perceived as a key driver of major depressive disorder pathogenesis; hence, targeting ferroptotic cascades may reveal novel therapeutic targets. This study evaluated the neuroprotective potential of the oral iron chelator deferasirox (DEF) against chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced depressive-like behaviors and cognitive deficits in Wistar rats. Methods: We specifically explored whether DEF could provide neuroprotection by targeting ferroptotic and oxidative stress pathways. Male Wistar rats were exposed to a 6-week CUMS protocol and treated with DEF (10, 20, or 40 mg/kg). Results: CUMS-exposed rats exhibited significant anhedonia, behavioral despair, and impaired spatial and recognition memory. Further analyses revealed a reduction in colonic and choroid plexus occludin, reflecting compromised structural integrity of both the intestinal and blood-CSF barriers, accompanied by enhanced hippocampal iron accumulation with increased Acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4), Acyl-CoA synthetase family member 2 (ACSF2), and citrate synthase expression, alongside exaggerated oxidative stress and deficient neuroprotective mediators, specifically BDNF and synaptophysin, and increased neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) deposition, collectively exacerbating neurodegenerative pathology. DEF treatment ameliorated most of these effects, significantly reducing iron deposition, attenuating ferroptosis-related signaling, reducing oxidative stress, diminishing the ongoing neurodegeneration, and replenishing the depleted pool of BDNF and synaptophysin, which was accompanied by a reduction in depressive-like symptoms and improved cognitive functions. Conclusions: These findings support a link between ferroptosis-related signaling and depression-like phenotypes, reinforcing the concept of a metal-driven component in depression pathophysiology and offering a mechanistic rationale for further exploring targeting ferroptotic pathways and central iron regulation as potential targeted strategies in depression management.

title: Comprehensive Preclinical Pharmacokinetic Characterization of FAD012, a Rationally Designed Ferulic Acid Derivative, Supports Its Further Development as a Cerebrovascular Protective Therapeutic Candidate for Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Background/Objectives: FAD012 (3,5-dimethyl-4-hydroxycinnamic acid), a ferulic acid (FA) derivative, exhibits greater cerebroprotective effects than FA in experimental cerebral ischemia. Prophylactic oral administration of FAD012 preserves cerebral blood flow and blood-brain barrier integrity, consistent with its protective effects on the cerebrovascular endothelium. Compared with FA, FAD012 has higher calculated lipophilicity and a lower topological polar surface area, suggesting altered membrane permeability and systemic disposition. However, its pharmacokinetic characteristics remain unclear. Methods: This study compared the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of FAD012 and FA in male Sprague-Dawley rats. After intravenous and oral administration (10 mg/kg), plasma concentration-time profiles were analyzed using compartmental pharmacokinetic models. Tissue distribution after 2 weeks of dietary administration and plasma protein binding were also evaluated. Results: After intravenous administration, FAD012 exhibited a longer elimination half-life and tended to have a larger volume of distribution than FA, without a significant difference in total clearance. After oral administration, FAD012 showed more rapid absorption, with a higher maximum plasma concentration and a shorter time to maximum plasma concentration, with no significant differences in the area under the concentration-time curve or absolute bioavailability. After chronic administration, unchanged FAD012 was present at a higher plasma concentration, alongside lower tissue-to-plasma concentration ratios. FAD012 also exhibited markedly higher plasma protein binding than FA. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that structural modification of FA to FAD012 alters absorption and systemic disposition without increasing absolute bioavailability. The higher plasma concentration of unchanged FAD012 observed after chronic administration may contribute to its cerebrovascular protective effects and support its potential as a prophylactically administered cerebroprotective agent for ischemic stroke.

title: Galantamine Ameliorates Doxorubicin-Induced Cognitive Impairment in Female Rats via Modulation of Neuroinflammation, BDNF/TrkB Pathway and Synaptic Plasticity.
abstract: Background: Chemotherapy-related cognitive impairment is a debilitating neurocognitive syndrome with no approved treatment. Doxorubicin induces neuroinflammation, disrupts neurotrophic signaling, and impairs synaptic plasticity. Galantamine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, has anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties. This study investigated the dose-dependent effects of galantamine (2.5 and 5 mg/kg) on cognitive behavior, neuroinflammation, the BDNF/TrkB pathway, and synaptic plasticity in a rat model of doxorubicin-induced cognitive impairment. Methods: Female Sprague Dawley rats were divided into control, doxorubicin (4 mg/kg/week, i.p.), doxorubicin + galantamine (2.5 mg/kg/day, oral), and doxorubicin + galantamine (5 mg/kg/day, oral) groups. After four weeks, spatial learning and memory were assessed using the Morris water maze, and recognition memory using the novel object recognition test. Hippocampal IL-1β, IL-10, BDNF, and AChE levels were measured by ELISA. Histopathology was assessed by H&E staining. TrkB expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry, and PSD-95 and synaptophysin by Western blot. Results: Doxorubicin impaired spatial learning and memory and reduced discrimination index in the NOR test. Galantamine, especially at 5 mg/kg, attenuated these deficits. Doxorubicin increased IL-1β and AChE, while decreasing IL-10 and BDNF. Galantamine at both doses reversed IL-1β and AChE increases and increased BDNF; only the 2.5 mg/kg dose increased IL-10. Doxorubicin-induced neuronal shrinkage and apoptosis were ameliorated by galantamine. Doxorubicin upregulated TrkB, which was normalized by high-dose galantamine. Western blot showed that doxorubicin increased PSD-95 and decreased synaptophysin; galantamine did not alter PSD-95 but reversed the synaptophysin decrease at low dose. Conclusions: Galantamine exerts dose-dependent neuroprotective effects against doxorubicin-induced cognitive impairment by reducing neuroinflammation, modulating BDNF and TrkB levels, and preserving presynaptic plasticity. These findings suggest galantamine as a potential option for preventing chemotherapy-related cognitive impairment.

title: Current Pharmaceutical Strategies for the Long-Term Management of Addiction.
abstract: Background: Substance use disorders (SUDs) are chronic, progressive brain diseases that result in continued liability to relapse, even after periods of abstinence. Objectives: This review synthesizes current evidence for a paradigm shift in addiction medicine: from suppression of acute drug effects to repair of the neurobiological substrates underlying relapse vulnerability. Method: We used medical databases to conduct an electronic search to identify the objectives. We reviewed in detail the existing pharmacotherapies for SUD, discussing their mechanisms of action, efficacy data, and limitations. We then reviewed novel drug classes that target resilience-promoting mechanisms to conclude a comprehensive roadmap for the management of addiction. Result: Novel drug classes that target resilience-promoting mechanisms, including GLP-1 receptor agonists that modulate mesolimbic dopamine signaling, orexin receptor antagonists that target stress-induced craving, kappa-opioid receptor antagonists that counteract stress-induced dysphoria, and corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) antagonists that normalize hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysfunction. Furthermore, agents that stimulate neuroplasticity (ibogaine, noribogaine, glutamate modulators) and agents that target neuroinflammation (endocannabinoid modulators, microglial inhibitors), and biological interventions, including immunopharmacotherapy and psychedelic-assisted therapies, are new strategies for long-term management of addiction. Conclusions: Long-term management of addiction should provide a comprehensive roadmap to the development of next-generation addiction therapeutics that restore neural circuit function and promote long-lasting resilience to relapse for medicinal chemists and neuroscientists.

title: Safety, Tolerability, Pharmacokinetics, and Immunogenicity of BXOS110, a Novel PSD-95 Inhibitor: A First-in-Human Trial.
abstract: Background/Objectives: BXOS110 is a first-in-class eicosapeptide designed to target the post-synaptic density protein 95 (PSD-95)-mediated signaling cascade, which plays a key role in ischemic brain injury. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase I trial, we evaluated the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity of BXOS110 in 86 healthy adults. Methods: Participants were assigned to receive either single ascending doses (SAD; 30-320 mg) or multiple ascending doses (MAD; 120-240 mg once daily for 10 days) via intravenous infusion. Plasma concentrations of BXOS110 were quantified using a validated liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry method. Pharmacokinetic parameters were derived from the concentration-time profiles using a standard non-compartmental analysis method. Safety and tolerability were assessed throughout the study using adverse events, vital signs, physical examinations, laboratory parameters, etc. Results: Pharmacokinetic analysis demonstrated approximately dose-proportional increases in peak plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the curve (AUC) across the SAD cohort (30-320 mg). No marked drug accumulation was observed in the MAD cohort. No serious adverse events were reported. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were generally mild or moderate in severity, occurring in 16.7% (SAD) and 30% (MAD) of BXOS110 recipients, compared to 7.1% and 16.7% in the respective placebo groups. The incidence of anti-drug antibody (ADA) positivity was low, with no apparent association between immunogenicity and TRAE occurrence. Conclusions: BXOS110 demonstrated a favorable safety and tolerability profile. Our findings support its continued clinical development, and we recommend further investigation of multiple-dose regimens not exceeding 240 mg/50 mL or body weight-based dosing to better balance safety and efficacy.

title: Isolation Methods Shape the Properties and Immunomodulatory Activity of Trichinella spiralis Larval Extracellular Vesicles.
abstract: Trichinella spiralis muscle larvae-derived extracellular vesicles (TsEV) are key mediators of host-parasite interaction, yet the impact of isolation protocols on their properties and function remains unclear. This study compared four TsEV isolation protocols differing in culture duration (20 h vs. 4 days) and medium composition (with or without fetal bovine serum, FBS). Dynamic light scattering revealed that FBS supplementation yielded small particles (average ~150 nm), whereas FBS-free protocols produced larger, more heterogeneous populations, particularly with extended culture. Proteomic analysis identified a constitutive protein core across all conditions, alongside protocol-specific proteins, with exportin-1 consistently more abundant under FBS-free conditions irrespective of culture duration. Functional assays in RAW 264.7 macrophages showed that TsEV induced both nitric oxide (NO) and arginase activity, but the magnitude and kinetics of these responses varied markedly depending on the protocol. Among the conditions tested, Protocol 3 (4 days without FBS) induced the highest NO levels, whereas Protocol 4 (4 days with FBS) showed the strongest potentiation of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced arginase. These divergent profiles likely reflect differences in EVs' size and cargo arising from distinct culture conditions, although the relative contribution of duration and medium composition could not be fully dissected. Our findings demonstrate that culture parameters profoundly influence TsEVs' properties and immunomodulatory capacity, underscoring the need for standardized isolation protocols.

title: Expansion of the Betanodavirus epinepheli (RGNNV)/B. pseudocarangis (SJNNV) Reassortant Strain (Family Nodaviridae) Range to the Suez Canal Region.
abstract: Viral nervous necrosis (VNN), caused by betanodaviruses, is a major constraint to marine finfish aquaculture worldwide. This study reports the first detection and molecular characterization of an RGNNV/SJNNV reassortant betanodavirus in farmed gilthead seabream (Sparus aurata) in the Suez Canal basin, Egypt. Four mortality episodes in two adjacent marine hatcheries affected fry from 12 days post-hatching through juveniles of seven months. Affected fish showed nervous signs, and brain histopathology revealed spongiform vacuolation and neurodegeneration. No parasitic or bacterial pathogens were detected. RT-qPCR and conventional RT-PCR detected betanodavirus RNA in clinically affected fry and juveniles and in brains of apparently healthy broodstock. In one hatchery, viral RNA was also detected in incoming well water. Partial RNA1 and RNA2 sequencing of a virus from a single adult fish identified a reassortant strain, designated EGY_Waf25, comprising RGNNV RNA1 and SJNNV RNA2. EGY_Waf25 clustered with Mediterranean and North African reassortant betanodaviruses but formed a distinct branch in RNA1-, RNA2-, and concatenated RNA1/RNA2-based analyses. Genetic distance analyses supported this placement while indicating local differentiation. These findings extend the recognized geographic occurrence of RGNNV/SJNNV reassortants to the Suez Canal basin and identify a potential regional biosecurity risk for Egyptian mariculture. Enhanced surveillance, routine broodstock screening, and water monitoring are recommended.

title: Glycine Supplementation Reduces Lesion Size and Parasite Burden in BALB/c Mice Infected with Leishmania mexicana.
abstract: Glycine, a non-essential amino acid, plays diverse biological roles, including antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities, cytoprotective effects, neurotransmitter functions, and potential anticancer properties. The potential of glycine supplementation in parasitic diseases, such as leishmaniasis, remains underexplored. Leishmania mexicana, a protozoan parasite, is a causative agent of cutaneous leishmaniasis, characterized by chronic lesions and significant immunopathology. This study investigates the impact of glycine supplementation on disease progression and parasite control in a BALB/c mouse model of L. mexicana infection. BALB/c mice were infected with L. mexicana and received glycine-supplemented drinking water ad libitum, beginning on the day of infection. Glycine supplementation exhibited a protective effect, as evidenced by significantly reduced lesion sizes and decreased parasite burdens. Cytokine profiling of spleen cells from glycine-treated mice revealed an immunomodulatory effect, characterized by increased interleukin-10 (IL-10) production and decreased tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) levels upon stimulation with L. mexicana promastigote antigens. In vitro studies showed that glycine supplementation inhibited promastigote and amastigote growth in a dose-dependent manner. Macrophages cultured in glycine-enriched media showed reduced parasite recovery from infected macrophages. Importantly, no cytotoxic effects were observed in cultured host cells. Histological analysis of tissue lesions showed a lower parasite burden and diminished inflammatory infiltrate in glycine-treated mice. The histological analysis of liver and kidney tissues from glycine-supplemented mice showed no detectable histopathological alterations in liver or kidney at the tested doses. These findings suggest that glycine may represent a promising anti-Leishmania agent for controlling disease progression. Glycine's dual ability to modulate host immune responses and directly inhibit parasite growth highlights the potential benefits of early glycine supplementation in cutaneous leishmaniasis.

title: Thermal Responses During Sequential Carbohydrate Gel and Caffeine Intake Assessed by Infrared Thermography: Differences by Sex and Body Mass Index.
abstract: Background/Objectives: This study aimed to evaluate infrared thermography (IRT)-assessed thermal responses during a sequential carbohydrate gel and caffeine protocol across body mass index and sex groups. We also investigated whether absolute supraclavicular temperature (Tscv) alone is sufficient to interpret brown adipose tissue (BAT)-related thermal responses and examined the contribution of reference-adjusted thermal parameters. Methods: Our study included 36 participants, with 12 individuals in each group: those with normal weight, overweight, and obesity. The experimental protocol lasted 120 min. Participants received carbohydrate gel, followed by 200 mg of caffeine at 45 min. We assessed Tscv, reference temperature (Tref), relative temperature (Trel), delta temperature (ΔT), estimated core temperature, blood pressure, and heart rate. Neither BAT activity nor energy expenditure was measured directly. The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07868302). Results: Mean Tscv increased from baseline during the carbohydrate phase (median increase at 45 min: 0.72 °C; p < 0.001), with no further significant change after caffeine administration. At 90-120 min, participants with obesity had lower Tscv and Tref than those with normal weight, whereas Trel, ΔT, and changes after caffeine administration did not differ, indicating differences in absolute temperature rather than in thermal responses. Mixed-effects models showed no significant time-by-group interactions. No consistent sex or hemodynamic differences were observed. Conclusions: Supraclavicular skin temperature may be influenced by regional adiposity and heat transfer and should not be interpreted as an independent indicator of BAT activity. Controlled studies are needed to clarify the utility of IRT in assessing diet-induced thermogenesis.

title: A Systematic Review of Neuroimaging Evidence on Human Milk Oligosaccharides and Neurodevelopment: Brain Structure, Metabolism, Mechanistic Insights, and Future Directions.
abstract: Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) are bioactive glycans that may influence neurodevelopment through microbiota-dependent and independent pathways. This systematic review critically evaluates neuroimaging evidence linking HMO exposure to brain structure, microstructural organization, and neurochemical profiles, integrating imaging-derived outcomes with proposed molecular mechanisms and assessing their translational relevance to human infants. PubMed, MEDLINE, and Scopus were systematically searched from database inception to November 2026 for human and animal intervention studies investigating HMO-associated neuroimaging outcomes. Evidence was narratively synthesized according to HMO composition, dosage, developmental stage, imaging modality, and methodological quality. Eight eligible intervention studies were identified, all involving neonatal piglets; no human intervention studies met the neuroimaging eligibility criteria. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy findings suggested that sialylated HMO formulations were associated with positive changes in selected cerebral metabolites. Combined HMO and lactoferrin supplementation was also associated with altered regional metabolite profiles, although their independent contributions remain uncertain. Structural MRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and myelin-sensitive imaging findings were heterogeneous, predominantly region-specific, and frequently nonsignificant. Potential mechanisms involving microbial metabolites, Sia availability, ganglioside metabolism, neural cell adhesion molecule polysialylation, neuroinflammation, and synaptic plasticity, remain hypothesis-generating rather than causally established. Current preclinical evidence suggests that HMO-containing interventions may influence selected neuroimaging outcomes but does not establish consistent improvements in neurodevelopment. Methodological heterogeneity limits cross-study comparisons and the absence of eligible human intervention studies limit clinical translation. Longitudinal investigations integrating neuroimaging, molecular profiling, and functional assessments are needed to clarify the imaging-based neurodevelopmental relevance of HMOs.

title: Clocking Impulses: Mealtime Intervention Shifts Impulsivity, Associated with Glucose Metabolism and Plasma Tyrosine.
abstract: Impulsive behaviour has a daily rhythm and is greater in the evening. This can have negative health consequences, such as disinhibited food intake in the evening, associated with metabolic disease and obesity. Therefore, interventions targeting evening impulsivity are key to improving health. Through the role of mealtime as a circadian cue, we conducted a secondary analysis of a Time-Restricted Eating (TRE) trial, comparing early versus late TRE to shift mealtime and subsequently internal daytime. We examined whether this shift affects impulsivity and, if so, whether this is related to tyrosine, dopamine's precursor, and glucose metabolism. Twenty-eight female participants (Age = 56.9 ± 9.75 years, BMI = 30.3 ± 2.84 kg/m2 [mean ± SD], 13/28 with impaired glucose metabolism (IFG/IGT)) completed this preregistered, randomised crossover study (Clinical Trials identifier: NCT04351672, Open Science Framework osf.io/fuqwz). We applied two TRE interventions for two weeks each, early (mealtime 08:00-16:00) and late (13:00-21:00), to induce an internal daytime shift. After each intervention, fasted plasma tyrosine was assessed, followed by an impulsive decision-making task. Firstly, individuals made more impulsive decisions during the internal evening (after eTRE) compared to the morning (after lTRE), determined by mealtime intervention (χ2 = 12.31, df = 1, p < 0.001, OR = 1.27, 95% CI [1.11, 1.46]). Furthermore, tyrosine was positively associated with impulsive decisions, particularly for those with IFG/IGT compared to normal glucose metabolism (NGT) (χ2 = 10.00, df = 1, p < 0.01, OR = 0.87, 95% CI [0.75, 1.00]). Finally, in individuals with IFG/IGT, tyrosine was positively associated with impulsive decisions across both internal morning and evening, with a stronger effect in the evening (χ2 = 14.15, df = 1, p < 0.01, OR = 1.51, 95% CI [1.22, 1.88]). This study presents mealtime shift as an alternative, behavioural intervention for curbing evening impulsivity. Furthermore, we highlight tyrosine and glucose metabolism as biologically relevant associations in our female population with overweight/obesity. Future studies should determine whether this intervention influences other impulsive behaviours, such as impulsive food intake, particularly in the context of metabolic disease such as type 2 diabetes. NCT04351672, date: 17 April 2020.

title: Inflamate® Modulates A1/A2-Associated Astrocyte Markers and Hepcidin-Related Iron-Regulatory Gene Expression in LPS-Stimulated Mouse Astrocytes.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Brain inflammation may alter astrocyte function and disrupt iron homeostasis. Hepcidin may link inflammatory signals to intracellular iron retention. In this study, we investigated whether Inflamate®, a multi-ingredient plant-based supplement, induces changes in both A1/A2-associated markers and hepcidin-related iron regulation in an astrocyte cell model of LPS-induced inflammation. Methods: Mouse astrocytes were treated with Inflamate® before LPS stimulation and compared to vehicle-treated cells under normal and inflamed conditions. We measured the expression of inflammation, astrocyte reactivity, and iron control genes using RT-qPCR. We also measured some cellular proteins and secreted inflammation signals. Results: Inflamate® reduced expression of C3 (an A1-associated marker) and increased expression of S100A10 (an A2-associated marker). This opposing response was accompanied by decreased gene expression levels of NOS2 and IL6 under LPS stimulation. Intracellular iNOS and C3 proteins, as well as secreted IL-6 and C3a, were also reduced under inflammatory conditions. In addition to these changes, Inflamate® lowered hepcidin gene expression levels under both normal and LPS-stimulated conditions and suppressed the LPS-induced increase in FTH1 (which encodes the ferritin heavy chain). There were no treatment-related changes observed in the expression of the TFRC (transferrin receptor 1) and SLC40A1 (ferroportin) genes. These results suggest specific changes in astrocyte markers and a suppressed response in hepcidin-related iron metabolism genes. Conclusions: Inflamate® induced changes in both A1/A2-associated marker patterns and the expression of genes regulating iron metabolism in cultured astrocytes. These findings provide a basis for further study of Inflamate® in models of neuroinflammation.

title: Sweet Rewards: Preferred Candy and Money Elicit Equivalent Reward Positivity Responses.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Food is a salient reward that can influence dietary behavior, but it is unclear whether neural responses to food rewards differ meaningfully from responses to other salient rewards, such as money. The current study examined whether reward responses, as measured by the reward positivity (RewP) event-related potential, differed between individually preferred food and monetary rewards. Methods: Two one-sided tests (TOST) of equivalence along with null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) were used to determine whether observed differences were practically equivalent or significantly different. Participants (N = 158) completed food, monetary, and performance-feedback versions of a computerized doors task while electroencephalography data were recorded. Participants earned an individually preferred candy during the food task and money during the monetary task, whereas the performance-feedback task provided no tangible reward. Based on prior research, TOST equivalence bounds were set to dz = 0.25. Results: Manipulation checks confirmed significant RewP effects across all three tasks. Paired-samples t-tests showed RewP amplitude did not significantly differ between food and monetary rewards, and equivalence testing demonstrated that responses were practically equivalent within the prespecified bounds. Monetary rewards elicited significantly larger RewP amplitudes than positive performance feedback, whereas the comparison between food reward and positive performance feedback was inconclusive, with insufficient evidence to establish either a difference or practical equivalence. Conclusions: Findings suggest an individually preferred food can elicit reward-related neural activity comparable to a monetary reward. Results provide preliminary support that food and monetary reward salience may warrant consideration when designing monetary-based interventions to improve dietary behavior. Future work relating neural reward responses to dietary intake will help determine the clinical significance of neural indices of food reward.

title: Gut Microbiota, Fecal Intestinal Biomarkers, and Dietary Factors Associated with Histamine-Related Symptom Phenotypes.
abstract: Background: Histamine-related symptoms are heterogeneous, and their associations with gut microbiota, intestinal biomarkers, and dietary factors remain incompletely understood. This study investigated relationships between selected bacterial taxa, fecal biomarkers, dietary habits, and individual symptom phenotypes. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 197 adults. Symptoms and dietary habits were assessed using questionnaires, while selected bacterial taxa were quantified by fecal qPCR. Fecal zonulin, calprotectin, and secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) were measured. Associations were examined using Spearman correlations, multivariable logistic regression, and principal component analysis (PCA), with false discovery rate (FDR) correction where applicable. Results: Headache/migraine was the most frequently reported symptom (60.9%). After FDR correction, headache/migraine severity correlated inversely with Faecalibacterium (ρ = -0.254; q = 0.024), flushing positively with Enterobacter (ρ = 0.249; q = 0.024), nausea inversely with Lactobacillus spp. (ρ = -0.234; q = 0.038), and pruritus positively with Firmicutes (ρ = 0.228; q = 0.038). Adjusted logistic models identified symptom-specific associations involving Lactobacillus spp., Enterobacter, and sIgA. Two PCA components explained 45.6% of bacterial variance, but their symptom associations did not survive FDR correction. Fermented dairy consumption correlated positively with gastrointestinal symptom severity (ρ = 0.269; q = 0.016) and inversely with Enterobacter abundance (ρ = -0.289; q = 0.010). Conclusions: Selected microbial taxa, mucosal immune activity, and dietary factors showed distinct associations with histamine-related symptoms. These exploratory findings require prospective validation.

title: The Caffeinated Brain Part 4: Effects of Caffeine on Human Functional MRI-Task-Evoked Brain Activity and Intrinsic Functional Networks: A Systematic and Mechanistic Review.
abstract: Caffeine is the most widely consumed psychoactive substance and primarily acts through antagonism of adenosine A1 and A2A receptors. Its effects are particularly relevant to functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), because caffeine influences both neuronal activity and cerebrovascular physiology, complicating interpretation of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal. This systematic and mechanistic review aimed to synthesize evidence on the effects of caffeine on task-evoked brain activity, resting-state functional connectivity, intrinsic BOLD dynamics, and neurovascular physiology in humans. A systematic search, reported as covering database inception through 4 July 2026, used PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, with supplementary bibliographic discovery and citation tracking. The published search concepts were translated into database-specific strings for reproducibility; the historical verbatim exports and source-specific counts require verification. Human caffeine-fMRI studies were synthesized qualitatively. Original RoB 2 and ROBINS-I judgments were reviewed for applicability to randomized, non-randomized intervention, and observational exposure designs; observational findings were interpreted separately where the original assessment instrument was unsuitable. Of 111 initially identified records, 39 publications were ultimately included. Caffeine did not produce a uniform increase or decrease in task-evoked BOLD activity. Instead, effects varied according to brain region, cognitive process, task load, habitual caffeine consumption, abstinence status, and physiological state. The most reproducible physiological effect was a reduction in resting cerebral blood flow, commonly by approximately 20-35%. Resting-state studies generally demonstrated reductions in positive functional connectivity and spontaneous low-frequency BOLD fluctuations, particularly within sensory and motor systems, while also showing redistribution of connectivity among large-scale networks, altered network anticorrelation, greater temporal variability, and increased BOLD signal entropy. Neuroimaging changes frequently occurred without corresponding behavioral improvements. Risk-of-bias assessments indicated generally more favorable methodological profiles for randomized crossover studies, whereas non-randomized studies were more susceptible to confounding and exposure-classification bias. Caffeine should not be regarded as a simple cerebral stimulant or BOLD contrast enhancer. Its fMRI effects emerge from interactions between adenosinergic neuronal modulation, altered arousal and network organization, and pronounced cerebrovascular effects. Consequently, changes in BOLD activity or functional connectivity cannot automatically be interpreted as proportional changes in neuronal activity. Future studies should combine standardized caffeine-exposure protocols with measurements of cerebral perfusion and complementary electrophysiological or multimodal imaging methods to better separate neuronal from vascular contributions to caffeine-related functional brain changes.

title: The Role of Monoamine Oxidases in ADHD: A Narrative Review of Plant-Derived Inhibitors.
abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is one of the most commonly diagnosed neurodevelopmental disorders, occurring in both children and adults, with its etiology and clinical presentation being multifactorial. Despite significant progress in diagnostics and treatment, available therapeutic strategies-particularly pharmacotherapy-are characterized by limited efficacy in some patients and the risk of numerous adverse effects. In recent years, natural bioactive compounds capable of modulating monoaminergic neurotransmission are gaining increasing interest; one of the mechanisms is the inhibition of the activity of monoamine oxidases (MAO-A and MAO-B), key enzymes involved in the metabolism of selected neurotransmitters. This paper provides a narrative review of the current state of knowledge on ADHD, covering its clinical characteristics, diagnostic process, currently used therapeutic methods, and the role of MAO enzymes in the regulation of central nervous system functions. Particular attention is devoted to natural MAO inhibitors, with an emphasis on plant-derived compounds. Due to the fact that the extraction and analysis of bioactive substances from flower petals remains a poorly explored area, this can be a significant research topic for developing new, potentially safer and better tolerated alternatives or adjuncts to conventional drugs used in ADHD therapy.

title: Caffeine and Experimental Pain Sensitivity in Humans-Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Acute caffeine may modify laboratory-evoked pain, but its relevance to clinical analgesia is uncertain. We systematically reviewed controlled experiments of caffeine administered alone in healthy humans, distinguishing pain intensity, threshold, tolerance, and induced hypoalgesia. Six databases were searched through 1 September 2026 using PRISMA 2020 methods. Nine experiments (216 analyzed participants) were included; five (130 participants) supplied pain-intensity contrasts for an exploratory REML random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. The pooled effect was uncertain (Hedges' g = 0.61, 95% CI -0.33 to 1.54; p = 0.146; I2 = 89.0%). Exclusion of the influential graph-derived cold-immersion estimate reduced g to 0.16 (95% CI -0.22 to 0.53; I2 = 24.7%). Pain threshold, tolerance, and induced hypoalgesia were not combined with pain intensity. Protocol differences could be described but not tested as reliable moderators. Adverse-event ascertainment varied substantially. The available evidence does not establish a consistent generalized hypoalgesic effect of caffeine alone. It can inform standardization of experimental pain research, but cannot justify caffeine treatment for clinical pain.

title: Plasma Ergothioneine Levels and Mushroom Consumption Are Associated with Lower Odds of Cognitive Impairment in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Findings from the Diet and Healthy Ageing (DaHA) Study.
abstract: Background: Cognitive impairment poses significant challenges to aging populations globally. Mushrooms, the primary dietary source of ergothioneine (ET), have been associated with cognitive health, but the specific roles of ET and its metabolite S-methyl-ergothioneine (S-ET) remain unclear. Objectives: This study intends to extend previous work on mushroom intake and cognition by simultaneously examining mushroom consumption, plasma ET, and plasma S-ET, and by exploring the independent associations and potential mediation or moderation roles of ET and S-ET in relation to cognitive impairment. Methods: Cross-sectional data from 499 older adults (67 ± 8 years, 75.35% female) from the "Diet and Healthy Ageing Study" (DaHA) in Singapore were analyzed. Cognitive impairment (CI) was defined as Modified Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score 2 servings/week was associated with lower odds of CI (OR = 0.421, 95% CI: 0.180-0.986). Higher plasma ET levels were also independently associated with lower CI odds. Exploratory moderation analyses suggested that the inverse association between mushroom intake and CI was more evident among individuals with higher ET or S-ET levels (Mushroom × ET interaction: β = -0.008, p = 0.007; Mushroom × S-ET interaction: β = -0.079, p < 0.05). No evidence of exploratory mediation was observed for either ET or S-ET. Conclusions: Higher mushroom intake and plasma ET levels were associated with lower odds of cognitive impairment. Exploratory analyses suggested that the mushroom-cognition association may vary according to ET and S-ET status. The findings on mushroom and ET/S-ET interaction and the lack of a mediating role in our cohort are preliminary and hypothesis-generating and require validation in future longitudinal and intervention studies.

title: Exploring Alcoholic Dementia: Integrated Bioinformatics of Alzheimer's Disease and Alcohol Use Disorder with Preliminary EGCG Evaluation.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a major cause of cognitive impairment, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying alcoholic dementia remain unclear. Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), the major catechin in green tea, has shown neuroprotective potential, but its targets in alcoholic dementia are undefined. This study aimed to explore disease-associated candidate molecular markers and potential EGCG-related targets in alcoholic dementia through integrated bioinformatics, machine learning, molecular docking, and experimental analyses. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) from GEO datasets GSE5281 and GSE62699 were subjected to functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, and machine learning-based feature selection. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, immune infiltration analysis, molecular docking, and experimental assays were subsequently performed. We identified 60 overlapping DEGs enriched in synaptic signaling, postsynaptic structure, GABA-A receptor activity, and cytokine receptor activity. IL-1R1 and ID3 were identified as candidate genes associated with immune infiltration, and both were upregulated in the hippocampus of ethanol-exposed mice. These findings highlight IL1R1 and ID3 as exploratory candidate genes and provide a preliminary basis for further investigation of EGCG in the context of alcohol-associated cognitive impairment.

title: Does Alcohol Type Matter? Investigating the Effects of Beer, Wine, and Liquor on Liver Health.
abstract: Purpose: Excessive alcohol intake is detrimental to liver health, but the differential impacts of types of alcohol on hepatic health remain understudied. Beer, wine, and liquor are the most common alcohols consumed worldwide, with each varying substantially in alcohol content and chemical profile, and given their popularity, an understanding of alcohol types and general liver health is needed. Search Methods: As such, we conducted a comprehensive narrative review focusing on pre-clinical and clinical studies on alcohol type and liver health by searching major research databases (PubMed, Google Scholar, Cochrane Library) for key terms associated with our topic and utilizing snowballing between August 2025 and September 2026. Search Results: Our search strategy yielded 301 total articles, of which 74 were included in the pre-clinical and clinical sections of this study, with 277 articles excluded. Discussion: Overconsumption of alcohol is detrimental to the liver regardless of type. Although some research indicates low and moderate red wine consumption is less deleterious, caution must be applied due to a variety of confounding factors. Liquor was found to be harmful to the liver across pre-clinical and clinical studies, while beer's impact was largely negative albeit varied based on many factors. Several gaps emerged, including a lack of studies on differing types of liquors, non-red wines, beers, and hard seltzers, as well as pre-clinical experiments in females. This review highlights that all alcoholic beverages may not uniformly impact the liver, and that more research is needed to determine how different alcohol types impact liver health.

title: Dietary GABA Remodels Hepatic Protein Networks and Lipid Droplet Architecture in Mice with Diet-Induced Hepatic Steatosis.
abstract: Dietary γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is a food-derived bioactive compound with potential metabolic benefits. However, its effects on hepatic protein networks and lipid droplet (LD) organization under high-fat diet (HFD)-induced steatosis remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the hepatic responses to dietary GABA supplementation in mice with HFD-induced hepatic steatosis. Male C57BL/6J mice with HFD-induced hepatic steatosis supplemented GABA orally at 180 mg/kg/day for 5 weeks. Hepatic responses were evaluated using label-free quantitative proteomics and scanning electron microscopy (SEM)-based analysis of LD morphology and spatial organization. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs; adjusted p 1) and protein-protein interaction networks were analyzed to characterize functional pathways and protein modules associated with GABA supplementation. Proteomic profiling identified 108 DEPs (38 upregulated, 70 downregulated), indicating changes in protein networks related to proteostasis, lipid metabolism, and immune- and stress-responsive processes. Protein-protein interaction analysis identified a hub module enriched in ubiquitin-dependent protein quality control components, including ubiquilin-1 (UBQLN1) and ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L3 (UCHL3), which showed reduced abundance following GABA supplementation. GABA also increased the abundance of LD-associated proteins, including perilipin-5 (PLIN5) and glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase 4 (GPAT4), while changes were also observed in immune- and stress-responsive proteins, including poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase family member 9 (PARP9). SEM revealed remodeling of hepatic LD architecture in HFD with GABA-supplemented mice compared with HFD mice, with reduced mean LD area (593.30 vs. 1267.24 μm2, p = 0.012), decreased nearest-neighbor distance (32.69 vs. 46.95 μm, p = 0.015), and increased perimeter-to-area ratio (0.17 vs. 0.12, p < 0.001). Total hepatic lipid content and body weight were not significantly altered. Dietary GABA supplementation was associated with remodeling of hepatic LD architecture and changes in protein networks related to proteostasis, lipid metabolism, and immune- and stress-responsive pathways, without reducing total hepatic lipid burden.

title: Late D-Chiro-Inositol Treatment Has Limited Effects on Hippocampal Alterations in Aged 3×Tg-AD Mice: Partial Rescue of CA1 Neurons Without Recovery of the Dentate Gyrus-CA3 Circuit.
abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder and the leading cause of dementia worldwide. Among the mechanisms implicated in AD progression, brain insulin resistance has been associated with impaired synaptic function and cognitive decline. In this context, inositols have emerged as promising neuroprotective compounds, and previous studies have reported beneficial effects of early D-chiro-inositol (DCI) administration in the 3×Tg mouse model. This exploratory study aimed to evaluate whether chronic oral DCI administration initiated at an advanced stage can modulate hippocampal neuronal density, synaptic markers and signaling pathways associated with insulin resistance in aged 3×Tg mice. Methods: Male and female wild-type and 3×Tg mice received DCI in drinking water (approximately 200 mg/kg/day) from 9 to 12 months of age. Neuronal density was assessed by unbiased counting of NeuN-positive cells (cells/mm2), and hippocampal protein expression was analyzed by Western blot, including markers related to insulin signaling, Tau phosphorylation, glutamatergic and endocannabinoid pathways, neuroinflammation and synaptic integrity. Sex effects were formally evaluated by three-way ANOVA (sex × genotype × treatment). Results: 3×Tg mice showed a lower neuronal density in the dentate gyrus-CA3 circuit, females displayed lower neuronal densities than males, and synaptophysin (males) and PSD95 (females) were reduced in 3×Tg mice. DCI increased neuronal density in the CA1 region of 3×Tg females but did not restore the neuronal deficit in the dentate gyrus-CA3 circuit or the synaptic markers. Compared with wild-type mice, 12-month-old 3×Tg animals displayed limited alterations in hippocampal signaling proteins, and DCI induced only sparse, often sex-dependent changes that neither normalized insulin signaling nor reduced Tau phosphorylation. Conclusions: Late-onset administration of DCI had limited effects on hippocampal alterations in aged 3×Tg mice. Although treatment ages were not directly compared, these findings contrast with previous results in which DCI treatment initiated at 3 months of age proved effective, and support the hypothesis that the therapeutic window for DCI narrows as pathology progresses. The sex-dependent differences observed further highlight the importance of considering sex as a biological variable in the design of therapeutic studies.

title: Development and Characterization of a Multi-Directional Light Dosimeter for Environmental Light Qualification: The Light Tracker.
abstract: Light is essential for several biological functions: it enables vision, regulates circadian rhythms, and influences neuroendocrine activity. However, both the quality and the quantity of light strongly determine its effects on the human body. Accurate characterization of light exposure in free-living conditions is therefore required to distinguish natural illumination from artificial sources. A common practice is to use 1000 lux as a threshold to differentiate outdoor from indoor conditions, and by extension natural versus artificial light. However, this categorization is unreliable, as it is highly sensitive to measurement conditions such as sensor orientation and shadowing. To overcome these limitations, we developed a multi-directional light dosimeter designed for seamless daily life use while capturing spatial variations in light and enabling robust environmental qualification. The Light Tracker is equipped with multiple spectral sensors positioned across different orientations to quantify directional dependence and identify the orientation that best represents a wearer's light environment. The device is USB-powered for ease of use in any context and is controlled through a dedicated mobile application. Characterization and calibration procedures employed controlled broadband sources, neutral-density filtering, and outdoor reference measurements to ensure the reliability of the collected data. Initial measurements demonstrate a strong angular dependence of absolute illuminance but higher stability of spectral ratios. They also highlight the robustness of the upward-facing side. Overall, the Light Tracker provides an effective tool for multi-dimensional light characterization, enabling real-world environmental classification and wearable photometric monitoring.

title: An Active LIDAR-Assisted Sensing System to Enhance Mobility for the Visually Impaired.
abstract: Echolocation enables individuals with impaired or no vision to recognize spatial features by analyzing sound reflections. However, acquiring this skill requires extensive training, and environmental factors influence its reliability. Moreover, users must continuously emit sounds while interpreting auditory feedback. In previous work, we introduced the LIDAR-Assisted Spatial Sensing (LASS) system, which detects the surrounding environment and translates it into stereo sound with varying pitches. Pitch encodes distance and stereo panning encodes direction, enhancing spatial perception. A key limitation of LASS is its passive scanning methodology: it restricts user control and requires a fixed 13-s full scan. In addition, the previous LASS evaluation was conducted with seated participants performing stationary localization judgments; it did not test whether the system could support closed-loop, mobile navigation. This paper presents an active LASS (ALASS) system that enables users to select regions of interest via a tactile handheld controller. This mechanism reduces regional scan time and gives users greater control, enabling adaptive scanning strategies similar to biological echolocation. A proof-of-concept study (N = 2) provides preliminary validation that ALASS supports closed-loop navigation in structured environments, where the user continuously senses, decides, and acts, steering based on audio feedback, with the resulting motion changing what the system subsequently senses.

title: A 5-Digit Manipulandum System to Measure and Train Finger Coordination During Object Manipulation.
abstract: Knowledge of how high-dimensional finger forces coordinate to achieve low-dimensional object manipulation is of fundamental interest in the field of sensorimotor neuroscience. We developed a novel 5-digit manipulandum integrating force sensors, actuators, and real-time software to measure and train finger force coordination within the conceptual framework of body-machine interfaces. The device enables personalized mapping between fingertip forces and two-dimensional cursor motions through a calibration process based on principal component analysis. In a proof-of-concept study, eight participants learned to maneuver a cursor across a planar target grid within 1 h of training. Significant improvements in movement time (p = 0.002) and path efficiency (p = 0.002) coincided with an increase in the planarity of digit-force coordination patterns (p = 0.001). The improvements in performance and the low-dimensional organization of digit-force coordination were consistent with short-term retention in the sense that performance values after a 6 h delay were comparable to those observed immediately after practice. The results demonstrate the system's potential as a research tool for studying hand motor control.

title: Culturable Microbial Communities in Winery Floors: Spatiotemporal Dynamics, Diversity, and Physiological Profiles.
abstract: Winery floors represent an important but poorly characterized component of the winery ecosystem and may act as reservoirs of microorganisms associated with grape processing and fermentation. This study investigated the spatiotemporal variation in culturable microbial communities inhabiting winery floors in three Portuguese wine regions (Douro, Alentejo and Vinhos Verdes) over four pre- and post-harvest sampling periods. Microbial density was assessed using culture-dependent methods, representative morphotypes were identified by Sanger sequencing, and community-level physiological profiles (CLPPs) were determined using Biolog EcoPlates. Microbial densities varied significantly according to winery, winery sector, culture medium and sampling period. Taxonomic analyses revealed a diverse cultivable microbiota comprising 87 genera, including 45 bacterial and 42 fungal genera. Several taxa were repeatedly recovered across wineries and sampling periods, suggesting the existence of a persistent cultivable component, whereas numerous genera were exclusive to post-harvest periods, indicating substantial harvest-associated community turnover. Functional profiling revealed significant spatial and temporal variation in substrate-utilization patterns. However, microbial abundance, taxonomic composition and functional responses were only partially coupled, with pre-harvest communities frequently exhibiting higher substrate utilization despite lower microbial densities. Canonical correspondence analysis identified significant associations between microbial genera and substrate-utilization profiles, highlighting winery-specific functional patterns. These findings demonstrate that winery floors harbour diverse and dynamic microbial communities shaped by both production activities and local environmental conditions, reinforcing the value of integrating abundance, taxonomic and functional approaches to characterize winery-associated microbiota.

title: Gut-Derived Metabolites Associated with Blood-Brain Barrier Alterations in Autistic Children: Preliminary Insights from a Sibling Pair Study.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) frequently co-occurs with gastrointestinal symptoms, motivating the investigation of microbial and metabolic factors within the microbiota-gut-brain axis. However, the effects of participant-derived faecal preparations on brain endothelial barrier properties remain incompletely characterised. This exploratory study combined gut and oral microbiota profiling, faecal metabolomics, and an endothelial resistance assessment in four sibling pairs discordant for ASD. Microbiota were analysed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and untargeted HPLC-ESI/HRMS metabolomics was performed in two sibling pairs. Faecal cell-free supernatants were tested in human brain microvascular endothelial cells using electrical resistance measurements complemented by an ATP-based viability assay. Participant-level microbial profiles showed substantial heterogeneity, and several differences apparent in group averages were not consistently reproduced across sibling pairs. Putatively annotated metabolic features were assigned to tryptophan-related pathways and the superpathway of chorismate metabolism; chorismate itself was not detected. Supernatants from the ASD participants in two of four pairs produced lower normalised endothelial resistance than the corresponding sibling control specimens, whereas this pattern was not observed in the other two pairs. No apparent reduction in ATP-based viability was observed at the measured endpoint. These findings integrate microbial and metabolic profiling with a functional endothelial assessment relevant to blood-brain barrier (BBB) research but do not establish an ASD-specific signature, BBB dysfunction, or a causal microbiota-metabolite-barrier mechanism. Larger, prospectively characterised cohorts and the controlled validation of candidate bioactive components are required.

title: Implementation of an Antimicrobial Stewardship Program in a University Hospital and Its Impact on Antibiotic Use and Clinical Outcomes: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance represents a major global health challenge, and hospital-based antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) are essential for promoting appropriate antibiotic use. This study aimed to introduce and implement an ASP in a university hospital and to assess its impact on antibiotic prescribing patterns and patient outcomes. We conducted a single-center study including infectious disease (ID) consultations performed before ASP introduction (2023), during implementation (2024), and after full implementation (December 2024-February 2025). Primary outcomes were carbapenem prescriptions and antimicrobial stewardship interventions, while secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, 30-day in-hospital mortality, and length of hospital stay (LOS). A total of 1673 ID consultations involving 975 patients in pre- and post-interventional phases were analyzed. Carbapenem prescriptions progressively and significantly declined over the study phases (from 32.1% to 18.6%; adjusted OR 0.57 [95% CI 0.35-0.92] in Phase II and 0.39 [95% CI 0.22-0.70] in Phase III compared to Phase I). Antimicrobial stewardship interventions increased significantly over time (reaching 54.0% in Phase III; adjusted OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.40-2.69). No significant differences in 30-day in-hospital mortality or LOS were detected across the study phases. In conclusion, a structured ASP was associated with improved antibiotic prescribing practices, supporting its role as a key strategy for optimizing antimicrobial use in hospital settings.

title: Histiocytoses in Children: Epidemiology, Clinical Spectrum, Molecular Pathogenesis and Treatment.
abstract: The histiocytoses are rare disorders driven by the clonal proliferation or pathological accumulation of cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system. The 5th edition of the WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours (2022) recognises Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and related entities as neoplasms derived from myeloid progenitors. This narrative review summarises current data on the epidemiology, clinical presentation, molecular pathogenesis, diagnosis and treatment of the histiocytoses most frequently encountered in children-LCH, juvenile xanthogranuloma, Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)-with emphasis on LCH. Mutually exclusive mutations of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway are found in 80-85% of LCH lesions, most frequently BRAF p.V600E (about 50% of paediatric cases), followed by MAP2K1 mutations and in-frame deletions or duplications of BRAF exon 12. BRAF p.V600E is associated with younger age, multisystem disease with risk-organ involvement, a poorer response to vinblastine-prednisone and LCH-associated neurodegeneration, although this association largely reflects disease extent rather than an independent prognostic effect. HLH, by contrast, is a syndrome of uncontrolled immune activation rather than a clonal disorder. Vinblastine and prednisone remain the backbone of LCH therapy, whereas BRAF and MEK inhibitors induce rapid responses in refractory and high-risk disease but seldom eradicate the mutated clone.

title: Research Progress on Exercise Combined with Micronutrients Regulating Oxidative Stress in Depression.
abstract: Depression is associated with interacting disturbances in oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial function, and synaptic plasticity. This structured narrative review examined how exercise and micronutrient status may modulate these processes through Nrf2/Keap1/ARE, IKK/NF-κB, MAPK, and JAK/STAT signaling. The original searches covered CNKI, PubMed, and Web of Science through December 2025; a targeted reference audit during revision produced an updated bibliography of 99 publications. Clinical studies support exercise-related improvement in depressive symptoms, whereas the proposed Nrf2, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and MAPK/CREB/BDNF mechanisms derive largely from experimental or single-intervention evidence and remain unconfirmed for combined treatment in patients. Zinc, selenium, magnesium, iron, and vitamin D participate in antioxidant enzymes, mitochondrial metabolism, neurotransmission, and immune regulation. The most defensible integrative model is conditional complementarity: adequate or corrected micronutrient status may enable a tolerable exercise stimulus to produce a fuller adaptive response. Direct factorial clinical evidence in depression is limited, so superiority of the combined approach is not established. Future trials should stratify participants by nutrient status and formally test interaction, mediation, dose-response relationships, and pathway-specific outcomes.

title: From Motor Neuron Monocultures to Human Neuromuscular Organoids: iPSC-Based Models of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) affects motor neurons, distal axons, skeletal muscle, and supporting cells.
